analysis.one_liner: Puts 80% of each year's federal budget surplus into personal retirement accounts for working Americans.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 1998 with six Republican cosponsors, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security subcommittee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: At the end of each fiscal year, the Treasury would move 80% of the federal budget surplus into a new Social Security Plus Fund and divide it evenly as personal accounts for everyone with a Social Security number who earned enough covered wages that year. The money would be invested under the same rules as federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan — broad index funds run by the government at low cost — and paid out at retirement as annuity-style payments. Regular Social Security benefits would continue unchanged; the accounts would be a supplement on top.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a Social Security number who works enough in a year to earn four quarters of Social Security coverage would get a flat deposit into a personal investment account, financed entirely by budget surpluses rather than payroll taxes. Because deposits are split evenly rather than by income, lower-wage workers would receive the same deposit as higher earners, and the government-run fund structure would keep management costs low.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wage earners with Social Security coverage

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible person would get an equal annual deposit from 80% of the total federal budget surplus, regardless of how much they earned above the minimum.

The fund would be invested and administered under the Thrift Savings Plan rules — the same low-cost index fund system used for federal employees — with independent audits, periodic statements, and fiduciary liability rules.

Deposits and earnings could not be spent on anything else; at retirement the balance must be paid out as life-expectancy installments or an annuity, and small balances under $3,500 (inflation-adjusted) could be taken as a lump sum.
If an account holder died before retirement age, the balance would pass to a surviving spouse or estate rather than disappearing.

analysis.who_pays: The federal budget surplus itself: 80% of it would be committed to the fund each year before any other use, such as debt reduction or other spending. Account holders would bear investment risk — net losses from the fund's investments would be allocated pro rata against individual account balances — and people without enough covered earnings in a year would get no deposit.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal budget surplus and lowest earners

drawbacks.text: Account holders bear the market risk: the bill credits net losses from fund investments against individual accounts pro rata, with no guaranteed return.
Eligibility requires earned income equal to at least four quarters of Social Security coverage in a year, so people with very little or no covered work in a year receive nothing.
The bill commits 80% of any total budget surplus every year before anything else is decided, locking up money that could otherwise go to debt reduction or other priorities.
Deposits cannot be touched until the account holder reaches old-age retirement benefits under Social Security, so the money is inaccessible for decades even in hardship.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is leaner than most Social Security privatization proposals: it leaves regular benefits untouched, adds a supplement funded by surpluses rather than diverting payroll taxes, and keeps investment inside a government-run, low-fee index fund system rather than handing accounts to private fund managers. The honest objections are real, though — account holders eat investment losses directly, the lowest earners are excluded, and committing 80% of every surplus year after year removes fiscal flexibility that an honest supporter would have to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and then its Social Security subcommittee, and it died there without a hearing, markup, or vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Kasich introduced the bill on March 12, 1998, and the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
On March 17, 1998, it was referred to the committee's Subcommittee on Social Security, where it remained.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one ever had to vote on committing the surplus, so the status quo held: budget surpluses of the late 1990s stayed available for other uses, and private money managers were spared a large new pool of retirement assets invested through a government-run, low-fee system.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Surplus status quo and private fund managers

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill; all seven sponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat is recorded as acting for or against it.

industries.note: The bill would route surplus investing through the federal Thrift Savings Plan structure — broad index funds run by the government at very low cost — leaving private fund managers with no role and no fees. Their interest in this design runs against account holders, who would pay far less under the government-run setup.

Retirement payouts must take the form of life-expectancy installments or an immediate annuity prescribed by regulation, potentially creating annuity purchase, though the bill does not clearly route payouts through private insurers. The fund may also buy fiduciary liability insurance.
